name: Cancún
tagline: Turquoise water, the biggest choice of resorts in Mexico, and the easiest flight in.
summary: Cancún's Hotel Zone is a long sand bar shaped like a 7, with the Caribbean on one side and the Nichupté lagoon on the other. It has the widest range of all-inclusive resorts in the country, a busy nightlife strip, and day trips to islands, Maya sites and cenotes. Downtown, a few minutes inland, is where locals eat and prices drop.
highlights: Calm, north-facing beaches between Playa Langosta and Playa Caracol
Snorkelling the underwater sculpture museum off Punta Nizuc and Isla Mujeres
Sunset over the lagoon from the Hotel Zone's west side
Tacos and markets in downtown Cancún (Mercado 28, Parque de las Palapas)
Day trips to Isla Mujeres, Chichén Itzá and the Ruta de los Cenotes
stay: Calmer, swimmable water and short ferry hops to Isla Mujeres.
Big resorts, wider beaches, closer to the airport.
Local prices and food; take the R1 bus to the beach.
tip: North-facing beaches near kilometre 4-9 of the Hotel Zone are sheltered and usually see less sargassum than the long east-facing stretch.

name: Costa Mujeres
tagline: Cancún's quiet new resort coast, facing Isla Mujeres.
summary: North of Cancún, Costa Mujeres is a newer strip of large all-inclusive resorts on a coastline that faces Isla Mujeres rather than the open sea. Water is generally calmer and the beaches are less crowded. The trade-off is that there is little outside the resorts, so most visitors eat and sleep on property and plan their outings.
highlights: Uncrowded resort beaches with views of Isla Mujeres
Short boat rides to Isla Mujeres and Isla Contoy bird sanctuary
Whale shark trips that leave from nearby marinas in summer
Golf and spa-focused resorts
Easy airport run without Hotel Zone traffic
stay: Self-contained all-inclusives; ideal for families and couples who want to unplug.
Ferry terminal area with local seafood restaurants.
Wild sandbar to the north, popular with kitesurfers.
tip: Book dinners in downtown Cancún or Puerto Juárez for a night out; taxis back are quick outside rush hour.

name: Isla Mujeres
transfer: 30 min to the ferry + 20 min crossing
tagline: A small island with shallow, glassy water and a slow golf-cart pace.
summary: Isla Mujeres is a narrow island a short ferry ride from Cancún. Playa Norte, at the north tip, has shallow, calm water you can wade into for a long way. Visitors get around by golf cart, ride out to the cliffs at Punta Sur, and in summer join licensed boats to swim with whale sharks. Staying overnight is the move: the island empties after the last day-trip ferries.
highlights: Wading at Playa Norte and sunset at its north end
Golf-cart loop to the cliffs and sculpture garden at Punta Sur
Whale shark tours from June to September
Snorkelling the reefs and the underwater sculpture museum
Fresh fish at the downtown waterfront and Mercado
stay: Walkable, near Playa Norte and the ferry.
Quiet lagoon side with boutique hotels.
tip: Ferries leave from Puerto Juárez (cheaper, more frequent) and the Hotel Zone. Stay at least one night to see the island after day-trippers leave.

name: Puerto Morelos
tagline: A fishing village with a protected reef a short swim from shore.
summary: Halfway between Cancún and Playa del Carmen, Puerto Morelos kept its small-town feel. Its reef is a national park and sits close to shore, so snorkelling is easy from licensed boats. A road inland known as the Ruta de los Cenotes leads to a string of freshwater sinkholes, and the town square has a laid-back food scene.
highlights: Snorkelling the Puerto Morelos Reef National Park
The leaning lighthouse and the town pier
Cenote-hopping along the Ruta de los Cenotes
Botanical garden with Maya-forest trails
Low-key seafood restaurants around the plaza
stay: Walk to the beach, pier and restaurants.
All-inclusives north and south of town.
Jungle cabins for a nature-first trip.
tip: Snorkel tours must use licensed guides and park wristbands; go in the morning when the water is calmest.

name: Playa del Carmen
tagline: The Riviera Maya's walkable hub, between Cancún and Tulum.
summary: Playa del Carmen grew around Quinta Avenida, a long pedestrian street of shops, cafés and bars a block from the sand. It is the most central base in the Riviera Maya: ferries cross to Cozumel, eco-parks and cenotes are a short drive away, and both Cancún and Tulum airports are reachable. Gated Playacar to the south is quieter and family-friendly.
highlights: Evening strolls on Quinta Avenida
Ferry day trip to Cozumel's reefs
Punta Esmeralda, a beach where a cenote meets the sea
Cenotes and eco-parks within 30 minutes
A wide food scene from street tacos to tasting menus
stay: Walk everywhere; can be noisy at night.
Gated resort area with calmer streets.
Newer condos and beach clubs north of centre.
tip: Beach width changes year to year; if the town beach is narrow, Punta Esmeralda and Xpu-Ha to the south are reliable alternatives.

name: Cozumel
tagline: Mexico's largest Caribbean island and one of the world's great drift dives.
summary: Cozumel sits on the Mesoamerican Reef, and its west coast is protected by a marine park famous for drift diving along walls such as Palancar and Columbia. The leeward side has calm water, while the wild east coast is for views rather than swimming. San Miguel, the only town, mixes cruise-day bustle with quiet evenings.
highlights: Drift dives and snorkelling in the Cozumel Reefs National Park
The rugged east coast drive with beach bars
Punta Sur reserve's lighthouse and lagoon
San Gervasio, the island's Maya sanctuary
Evening malecón in San Miguel
stay: Walkable town with restaurants and dive shops.
Closest to the best reefs and beach clubs.
tip: Swim and snorkel on the west side only; the east coast has strong currents. Cruise-free days are noticeably calmer in town.

name: Puerto Aventuras
tagline: A marina community made for easy family holidays.
summary: Puerto Aventuras is a planned marina town between Playa del Carmen and Tulum. It is quiet, safe-feeling and compact, with a golf course, a marina lined with restaurants and calm beaches inside a protected bay. Families use it as a base for cenotes, Xpu-Ha beach and the eco-parks without the crowds of the bigger towns.
highlights: Calm bay beaches for young swimmers
Marina dining and sport-fishing charters
Xpu-Ha beach a few minutes south
Cenotes along the highway towards Tulum
Nine-hole golf inside the community
stay: Condos and restaurants on the water.
tip: Rent a car for day trips; the highway gives you Akumal, Tulum and a dozen cenotes within 30 minutes.

name: Akumal
tagline: Swim beside green sea turtles in a sheltered bay.
summary: Akumal means place of turtles in Maya, and green sea turtles graze on the seagrass of its bay year-round. Swimming with them is now regulated: designated zones, life vests and certified guides. Next door, Half Moon Bay and the Yal-Kú lagoon offer calm snorkelling, and the area stays low-rise and relaxed.
highlights: Guided snorkelling with green sea turtles in Akumal Bay
Yal-Kú lagoon where fresh and salt water meet
Half Moon Bay's villas and reef
Cenotes on the west side of the highway
Easy hops to Tulum and Puerto Aventuras
stay: Villas and condos on a quieter cove.
tip: Arrive early, hire a certified guide, never touch or chase turtles, and use mineral sunscreen or a rash guard.

name: Tulum
tagline: Maya ruins above the sea, jungle cenotes and a design-led beach road.
summary: Tulum combines a walled Maya city on a cliff over the Caribbean with a beach road of boutique hotels and some of the most famous cenotes on the peninsula. The town, a few kilometres inland, has the better-value food and stays. Tulum has its own international airport and a Tren Maya station, which makes it easier to reach than it used to be.
highlights: The cliff-top Maya ruins at opening time
Gran Cenote, Dos Ojos and Calavera cenotes
Cycling between town and the beach
Day trip to the Sian Ka'an biosphere
Wellness retreats, temazcal and yoga
stay: Boutique hotels on the sand; highest prices.
Newer condos between town and beach.
tip: The beach and ruins area sits inside a national park with an entry fee. Carry cash for cenotes, and reach the ruins at opening to beat heat and crowds.

name: Sian Ka'an
tagline: A UNESCO biosphere of lagoons, mangroves and empty coast.
summary: South of Tulum, the Sian Ka'an Biosphere Reserve protects lagoons, mangroves, reef and forest. Visitors float through ancient Maya canals at Muyil, watch dolphins and birds on the lagoons, and stay in rustic lodges or the fishing village of Punta Allen at the end of a long, bumpy road. It is the Caribbean before resorts.
highlights: Floating the Maya canals at Muyil
Boat tours for dolphins, manatees and birds
Fly-fishing and lobster lunches in Punta Allen
Empty beaches along the reserve road
Night skies with no light pollution
stay: Eco-lodges between Tulum and Punta Allen.
tip: Go with a licensed local cooperative; the road is slow and services are thin, so bring cash, water and repellent.

name: Bacalar
tagline: The lagoon of seven colours: freshwater that looks like the Caribbean.
summary: Bacalar is a long, narrow freshwater lagoon whose bands of blue give it the name Lagoon of Seven Colours. There is no surf and no seaweed, just clear water for paddling, swimming and sailing. Its shallows hold stromatolites, rare living rock formations, so visitors are asked to skip sunscreen in the water and stay off them.
highlights: Sunrise kayak or paddleboard on the lagoon
Sailing to the Pirate Channel and Bird Island
Swimming in Cenote Azul and the Los Rápidos current
The 18th-century San Felipe fort
Lakeside cabins and slow evenings
stay: Walk to the fort, restaurants and docks.
tip: Water colours are strongest on sunny mornings. Protect the stromatolites: no walking on them and no chemical sunscreen in the lagoon.

name: Mahahual
tagline: A barefoot village on the Costa Maya with a world-class atoll offshore.
summary: Mahahual is a small town on the southern Costa Maya with a sandy malecón, beach bars and reef right off the shore. Divers use it to reach Banco Chinchorro, a protected atoll. It gets busy on cruise days and very quiet on the rest. This stretch of coast is among the most exposed to sargassum, so timing matters.
highlights: Snorkelling straight from the beach
Diving trips to the Banco Chinchorro reserve
A car-free beachfront malecón
Fresh ceviche and lobster in season
Day trip to Bacalar's lagoon
tip: Check sargassum reports and the cruise schedule before booking; winter months are usually the cleanest.

name: Holbox
tagline: A car-free island of sand streets, flamingos and whale sharks.
summary: Holbox is a sandbar island inside the Yum Balam reserve, reached by ferry from Chiquilá. Streets are sand, transport is golf carts and bikes, and the water is shallow and milky-green rather than deep blue. Summer brings whale sharks offshore; on dark nights the shallows can glow with bioluminescence.
highlights: Whale shark tours from June to September
Walking out to the Punta Mosquito sandbar
Flamingos and birds on the lagoon side
Bioluminescence on moonless nights
Lobster pizza and hammocks over the water
stay: Close to the ferry and restaurants.
Beach hotels east and west of town.
tip: Bring cash: ATMs are few and often empty. Leave the car in Chiquilá's guarded lots.

name: Mérida
tagline: The Yucatán's elegant capital and a base for ruins, cenotes and haciendas.
summary: Mérida is a colonial city of pastel mansions, plazas and free cultural events, and one of Mexico's most popular places for foreigners to live. It is the best base for the Puuc route and Uxmal, cenotes such as Cuzamá, hacienda stays and the Gulf beach at Progreso. April and May are very hot; winter is ideal.
highlights: Paseo de Montejo mansions and the main plaza
The Gran Museo del Mundo Maya
Uxmal and the Puuc route
Cenote circuits south of the city
Yucatecan cooking: cochinita pibil, sopa de lima, panuchos
stay: Colonial houses with pools; walk to plazas.
Modern area near malls and Progreso road.
tip: Sightsee early and late, rest at midday. Sunday brings street markets and live music around the main square.

name: Valladolid
tagline: A colonial town ringed by cenotes and the closest base to Chichén Itzá.
summary: Valladolid is a calm Pueblo Mágico with a cenote in the middle of town and dozens more nearby. It is the smartest base for Chichén Itzá and Ek Balam, letting you arrive at opening time before the tour buses from Cancún. Prices are much lower than on the coast.
highlights: Chichén Itzá at opening time
Climbing Ek Balam's great pyramid views
Cenotes Zací, Suytun and Ik Kil
The Calzada de los Frailes street
Yucatecan cooking at the municipal market
stay: Colonial hotels around the main square.
Boutique stays on the prettiest street.
tip: Sleep in Valladolid the night before Chichén Itzá and be at the gate when it opens.

name: Celestún
tagline: Flamingo lagoons and a fishing village on the Gulf.
summary: Celestún is a fishing town on a biosphere reserve where flamingos feed in shallow lagoons, most visibly in the cooler months. Boat tours run through mangroves, a petrified forest and freshwater springs. The beach is long, quiet and lined with seafood shacks.
highlights: Flamingo boat tours in the Ría Celestún reserve
Mangrove tunnels and a freshwater spring
Seafood on the beach
Sunsets over the Gulf
Day trip from Mérida with hacienda stops
tip: Use the official boat cooperatives at the bridge and ask the captain to keep a respectful distance from the flocks.

name: El Cuyo
tagline: A sleepy kite-surf village at the edge of a flamingo reserve.
summary: El Cuyo is a small fishing village on Yucatán's north coast, inside the Ría Lagartos area. Steady wind makes it a kitesurfing spot, the beach is long and empty, and boat trips go out to flamingos and mangroves. The pink salt ponds of Las Coloradas are nearby but are an industrial site with guided access.
highlights: Kite and wing-foil lessons
Flamingo and crocodile boat trips in Ría Lagartos
Long empty beaches
Las Coloradas pink lakes with an official guide
Seafood in the village square
stay: Cabins and small hotels on the sand.
tip: Pack for wind; afternoons can be breezy. Las Coloradas only allows guided visits on set paths.

name: Campeche
tagline: A walled pastel port city with UNESCO status and few crowds.
summary: Campeche's historic centre, built behind walls against pirates, is a UNESCO World Heritage site of colourful streets and bastions. A long malecón runs along the Gulf, and the Edzná ruins are an easy trip. Further inland, the Calakmul jungle site rewards a long day or overnight.
highlights: Walking the city walls and bastions
Sunset on the malecón
Edzná's five-storey pyramid
Calakmul's jungle pyramids
Seafood cocktails and pan de cazón
tip: Calakmul is far from everything; overnight nearby to reach the ruins early when wildlife is active.

name: Puerto Vallarta
tagline: Jungle mountains, a lively old town and whales in the bay.
summary: Puerto Vallarta wraps around Banderas Bay with the Sierra Madre rising behind it. The Malecón seafront and the Zona Romántica old town are full of restaurants, galleries and bars, and the city is known as one of Mexico's most LGBTQ+-welcoming destinations. Boats run to the Marietas Islands and to Yelapa, and humpback whales arrive in winter.
highlights: Sunset on the Malecón
Zona Romántica food and Los Muertos pier
Humpback whale tours from December to March
Boat to Yelapa or the Marietas Islands
Jungle hikes and river swims around Mismaloya
stay: Larger resorts between town and marina.
tip: Hidden Beach on the Marietas Islands has limited daily permits; book a licensed tour well in advance.

name: Nuevo Vallarta
tagline: Wide, flat beaches and big family resorts on the Nayarit side of the bay.
summary: Nuevo Vallarta is a planned resort area just across the state line from Puerto Vallarta. Its long, gently sloping beaches and large all-inclusives make it a favourite for families, and it has a marina and several golf courses. It is close to the airport and a short ride from Bucerías and Puerto Vallarta's old town.
highlights: Easy swimming beaches for kids
Turtle hatchling releases at resorts in season
Golf and marina life
Whale watching from the marina
Quick trips to Bucerías and Sayulita
tip: Afternoon wind picks up most days; plan beach time for the morning and the pool after lunch.

name: Bucerías
tagline: A friendly beach town with kite winds and long sunset walks.
summary: Bucerías is a relaxed town on Banderas Bay with a long beach, a weekly art walk and plenty of seafood. Afternoon winds make it a kitesurfing hub, and many North American retirees spend winters here. It is cheaper and calmer than Puerto Vallarta while still close to everything.
highlights: Kitesurfing lessons in the afternoon breeze
Long beach walks to Nuevo Vallarta
Art walk and street food in the evenings
Shrimp and fish tacos on the plaza
Easy hops to Punta Mita and Sayulita
stay: Walk to the plaza and beach.
Condos on the beach south of town.
Quieter rentals near Playa Destiladeras road.
tip: Look for monthly winter rentals; Bucerías is one of the bay's best-value places for long stays.

name: Punta Mita
tagline: The bay's luxury peninsula, with gentle surf and island boat trips.
summary: Punta Mita sits on the northern tip of Banderas Bay. Much of it is a gated luxury development with five-star resorts, private villas and oceanfront golf. Next to it, the public village of Punta de Mita has seafood restaurants, beginner-friendly surf at El Anclote and boats to the Marietas Islands.
highlights: Oceanfront golf and private beach clubs
Beginner surf at El Anclote
Boat trips to the Marietas Islands
Humpback whales close to shore in winter
Seafood at the village palapas
stay: Newer resorts and a quieter beach.
tip: Even if you stay elsewhere, the village side is public: surf lessons and seafood lunches cost a fraction of resort prices.

name: Sayulita
tagline: A colourful surf town with a big personality.
summary: Sayulita is a Pueblo Mágico known for beginner-friendly waves, colourful streets and a busy food and bar scene. It can be crowded in high season, and after heavy rains the river can affect water quality near the main beach. Quieter coves like Playa de los Muertos are a short walk away.
highlights: Surf lessons on the main break
Walk to Playa de los Muertos and Playa Carricitos
Taco stands and smoothie bowls
Jungle yoga retreats
Day trips to San Pancho and Punta Mita
stay: Right in the action; can be loud.
tip: After heavy rain, swim away from the river mouth or head to the southern coves.

name: San Pancho
tagline: Sayulita's quieter neighbour, with sunsets and a strong community spirit.
summary: San Francisco, known to everyone as San Pancho, is a small town with a long beach, wide sunsets and an active community centre. It suits travellers who want good food and a slower pace. The surf has strong currents, so it is more for watching than swimming on big days.
highlights: Sunset from the beach palapas
Yoga and wellness retreats
Farm-to-table restaurants on the main street
Community events and art classes
Short trip to Sayulita's nightlife
stay: Walk to the beach and restaurants.
tip: Watch for rip currents; ask locally which part of the beach is calm that day.

name: Puerto Escondido
tagline: Big-wave legend with calm coves, turtles and glowing lagoons.
summary: Puerto Escondido is famous for Zicatela, a powerful beach break that draws expert surfers, but most visitors swim in sheltered coves like Carrizalillo and Puerto Angelito. Evenings bring turtle hatchling releases in season, and at night boats cross the Manialtepec lagoon to see bioluminescence. It remains good value for the Pacific.
highlights: Watching big-wave surfers at Zicatela
Swimming at Carrizalillo cove
Baby turtle releases at sunset
Bioluminescence on the Manialtepec lagoon
Beginner surf lessons at La Punta
tip: Zicatela is for experts only. Swim at Carrizalillo or Puerto Angelito and check flags.

name: Mazunte
tagline: A tiny Pueblo Mágico of yoga, turtles and a cliff-top sunset.
summary: Mazunte is a small beach village on the Oaxaca coast, once a turtle-processing town and now home to a national turtle centre. Travellers come for yoga, simple cabañas and the sunset at Punta Cometa. Neighbouring San Agustinillo and Zipolite add more beaches within a few minutes.
highlights: Sunset hike to Punta Cometa
The Mexican Turtle Centre
Swimming at San Agustinillo
Yoga and wellness retreats
Whale and dolphin boat trips in winter
stay: Small hotels on a calmer bay.
tip: There are few ATMs; bring cash from Puerto Escondido or Huatulco.

name: Huatulco
tagline: Nine bays of calm water, a national park and coffee in the hills.
summary: Huatulco is a planned resort area spread across nine bays and more than thirty beaches, many protected inside a national park. Water in the bays is calm and clear, development is low-rise, and the town of La Crucecita keeps it grounded. Coffee farms in the Sierra Madre hills make a cool day trip.
highlights: Bay-hopping boat tour with snorkel stops
La Entrega and Maguey beaches
Huatulco National Park trails
Coffee farm tours in Pluma Hidalgo
Evening plaza life in La Crucecita
stay: Town hotels with the best value.
tip: Take the bay tour early; afternoon wind can make the outer bays choppy.

name: Los Cabos
transfer: 15 min to San José, 45 min to Cabo San Lucas
tagline: Desert meets sea at the tip of Baja: arches, whales and big sunsets.
summary: Los Cabos covers Cabo San Lucas, the resort Corridor and San José del Cabo at the southern tip of the Baja peninsula. It is dry and sunny almost all year, with world-class golf, sport fishing and luxury resorts. Many beaches are too rough for swimming, so it pays to know which ones are safe.
highlights: Boat to El Arco and Lover's Beach
Whale watching from mid-December to mid-April
Snorkelling at Chileno and Santa María bays
San José del Cabo's art district
Sport fishing and desert ATV trips
stay: Luxury resorts and the best swimmable bays.
Historic town, galleries and a calmer pace.
tip: Swim only at beaches signed as swimmable, such as Médano, Chileno and Santa María. On the Pacific side, waves and undertow are dangerous.

name: Cabo Pulmo
tagline: A tiny village beside one of the world's great marine-reserve recoveries.
summary: Cabo Pulmo National Park protects a coral reef in the Sea of Cortez. After the local community stopped fishing and backed the park, fish life rebounded dramatically, and it is now a celebrated example of ocean recovery. Divers see schools of jacks, sea lions and rays. The village is off-grid and simple.
highlights: Diving with huge schools of jacks
Snorkelling with licensed local operators
Sea lion colony at El Bajo
Empty East Cape beaches
Star-filled desert nights
tip: Book dives with park-licensed operators, bring cash and fuel, and expect patchy phone signal.

name: Todos Santos
transfer: about 1.5 h (or 1 h 15 from La Paz)
tagline: An artists' oasis town on Baja's Pacific coast.
summary: Todos Santos is a Pueblo Mágico of galleries, historic buildings and farm-to-table restaurants, set between desert mountains and the Pacific. Surfers head to Cerritos and San Pedrito, and whales pass offshore in winter. The ocean here is powerful, so swimming is limited to a few beaches.
highlights: Galleries and the historic town centre
Beginner surf at Playa Cerritos
Whale spotting from the beach in winter
Seasonal turtle releases
Farm-to-table dining
tip: Most Pacific beaches here have dangerous currents; swim at Cerritos and only when lifeguards are present.

name: La Paz
tagline: A real seaside city with sea lions, whale sharks and Balandra's shallows.
summary: La Paz, the capital of Baja California Sur, is a relaxed waterfront city with a long malecón. From here, boats reach Espíritu Santo island to swim with sea lions, and regulated tours visit whale sharks in the bay during the cooler months. Balandra's turquoise shallows are among Mexico's most photographed beaches.
highlights: Swimming with sea lions at Los Islotes
Kayaking and camping on Espíritu Santo
Whale sharks in the Bay of La Paz (October to April)
Balandra beach's shallow lagoon
Sunset on the malecón
stay: Walk to restaurants and tour docks.
Marina resorts on the way to Balandra.
tip: Balandra has visitor caps and time slots; arrive early and check the current rules.

name: Loreto
tagline: Blue whales, island kayaking and the oldest mission in the Californias.
summary: Loreto is a small Pueblo Mágico on the Sea of Cortez, beside a national marine park. In late winter, blue whales, the largest animals on Earth, feed in the bay. Its 17th-century mission was the first in the Californias, and the islands offshore are made for kayaking and snorkelling.
highlights: Blue whale tours in February and March
Kayak and snorkel trips to Isla Coronado
The historic mission and plaza
Hikes in the Sierra de la Giganta
Gray whale day trips to Magdalena Bay
stay: Resort and marina area south of town.
tip: Whale tours use licensed local pangas with strict approach rules; book a morning slot when the sea is flattest.

name: Puerto Peñasco
tagline: Arizona's beach: a drivable Sea of Cortez escape.
summary: Known to Americans as Rocky Point, Puerto Peñasco is the closest beach to Arizona, a few hours' drive from Phoenix and Tucson. Huge tides expose tide pools, condo resorts line Sandy Beach, and the El Pinacate desert reserve sits inland. Winters are cool and the water cold; late spring and autumn are best.
highlights: Tide-pooling at low tide
Sandy Beach condo resorts
The Malecón fish market
El Pinacate's volcanic craters
Sunset cruises and fishing
tip: Buy Mexican auto insurance before you cross, and check the current vehicle-permit rules for Sonora.

name: Valle de Guadalupe
tagline: Mexico's wine country, an hour from the Pacific.
summary: Valle de Guadalupe, inland from Ensenada, produces most of Mexico's wine. Its wineries range from family cellars to architect-designed estates, and its outdoor restaurants helped put Baja cuisine on the map. Ensenada's fish tacos and the La Bufadora blowhole are nearby.
highlights: Winery tastings on a guided route
Outdoor tasting-menu restaurants
August harvest festivals
Fish tacos and markets in Ensenada
La Bufadora marine geyser
tip: Hire a driver for tasting days; distances between wineries are longer than they look, on dirt roads.

name: Mexico City
tagline: A megacity of museums, markets and some of the world's best food.
summary: Mexico City combines Aztec ruins, a UNESCO-listed historic centre, leafy neighbourhoods like Roma and Condesa, and one of the planet's great food scenes. It is a natural stopover on the way to the coasts. The city sits around 2,240 metres up, so take it easy the first day.
highlights: Templo Mayor and the Zócalo
The National Museum of Anthropology
Roma and Condesa food crawls
Frida Kahlo's Casa Azul in Coyoacán
Teotihuacan pyramids at sunrise
tip: Book Casa Azul tickets online well ahead, and use authorised airport taxis or app rides.

name: Oaxaca City
tagline: Mole, mezcal and mountain ruins in Mexico's craft capital.
summary: Oaxaca's historic centre and the hilltop city of Monte Albán are a joint UNESCO site. The city is famous for moles, mezcal, markets and weaving villages, and for two festivals that pack hotels: the Guelaguetza in July and the Day of the Dead. Pair it with the Oaxaca coast by a short flight or a scenic drive.
highlights: Monte Albán's mountaintop ruins
Santo Domingo church and gardens
Mercado 20 de Noviembre's grill hall
Hierve el Agua petrified waterfalls
Mezcal distilleries in the valleys
stay: Walk to churches, markets and restaurants.
tip: For the Guelaguetza or Day of the Dead, book rooms and event tickets months ahead.

name: San Miguel de Allende
tagline: A rose-pink parish church, rooftop sunsets and a big creative community.
summary: San Miguel de Allende is a UNESCO-listed colonial town known for its pink neo-Gothic parish church, art schools and a large community of foreign residents. It suits slow travel: galleries, hot springs, cooking classes and rooftop dinners. It sits about 1,900 metres high, so evenings are cool.
highlights: The Parroquia at golden hour
Fábrica La Aurora art centre
Hot-spring pools outside town
Atotonilco sanctuary
Rooftop bars over the jardín
tip: Streets are steep cobblestone; pack comfortable shoes and allow time to adjust to altitude.

name: Guanajuato
tagline: A colourful silver-mining city of tunnels, alleys and music.
summary: Guanajuato is a UNESCO-listed city built in a ravine, with roads running through old tunnels beneath its colourful houses. Students keep it lively, musicians lead singing walks through the alleys at night, and the Cervantino arts festival takes over every October.
highlights: The funicular to the Pípila lookout
Callejoneadas: night walks with musicians
Callejón del Beso
Diego Rivera's birthplace museum
Underground streets and tunnels
tip: Hotels fill fast during the Cervantino in October; book early.
